blocks.title: Building the session and the week

summary.title: The programme variables
points: Seven dials: exercise, sets, reps, load, rest, tempo, frequency.
The key summary is hard sets per muscle group per week: your volume.
Hard sets end roughly 0–3 reps from failure.
Change one dial at a time and give it 3–4 weeks.

exercises.scenario: You decide to change your programme after a dull month.

options: Training at another time of day
New exercises, more sets and shorter rest, all at once to shock the body
A completely different programme from a magazine
Same plan, 4 sets of squats instead of 3
questions.explanation: Then you can tell what helped.

questions.prompt: Which set counts as a hard set?
options: 10 reps with about 2 left in reserve
A warm-up set of 10 with about 8 reps left in reserve
A set stopped halfway because the phone rang

exercises.scenario: A friend counts 'total kilos lifted' each week.

options: Hard sets per muscle group per week
Calories burned during each session according to a watch
questions.explanation: It's what the volume research counts.

questions.prompt: How long should a dial change run before you judge it?
options: One session, so you can switch quickly if it feels wrong

summary.title: Effort: RPE, RIR, failure
points: RIR: reps left. RPE 10 = 0 left, 9 = 1, 8 = 2.
Usual working zone: 1–3 reps in reserve (RPE 7–9).
Failure gave only a trivial growth advantage overall (2023 meta-analysis), and costs more fatigue.
People underestimate reps left by about one.
Calibrate now and then with a set to failure on a safe exercise.

exercises.scenario: You finish 12 push-ups and feel you had 'about 3 left'.

options: About RPE 10, since push-ups always feel hard by the end
You had exactly 3 left, since estimates are always precise
You may have had a bit more than you think
questions.explanation: Most people underpredict by about one rep.

exercises.scenario: A friend takes every set of squats to total failure.

options: Failure on every set is required for any muscle growth to happen
Failure isn't needed and adds fatigue
questions.explanation: A trivial advantage overall; 1–3 RIR is enough.

questions.prompt: Where is going to failure safest for calibration?
options: Heavy goblet squats with the heaviest bell you own
Push-ups or other safe bodyweight moves
questions.explanation: Low risk if the last rep fails.

summary.title: Volume: sets per week
points: Muscle growth rises with weekly sets, with diminishing returns (2026 meta-regression).
About 4 weekly sets already made a measurable difference; strength levelled off after about 3–4.
ACSM 2026: about 10 sets per muscle group per week for growth.
Count helpers as half a set (push-ups: chest 1, triceps 0.5).
Start at 6–10, rise towards 10–15 if recovery is good and progress stalls.

exercises.scenario: Each week: 3 sets of push-ups and 3 of floor press.

options: 3, since only push-ups count for the chest

questions.prompt: Sets for the triceps, counting helpers as half?
options: 6, since every pushing set counts fully for the triceps

exercises.scenario: You want maximal strength more than size this block.

questions.prompt: What does the volume evidence suggest?
options: Strength needs more volume than size
Volume has no effect on strength at all
Strength needs at least 25 weekly sets per muscle to improve
Strength levels off at fairly few weekly sets
Every week, regardless of how you're recovering
When progress stalls and recovery is good

summary.title: Frequency: full-body A/B
points: Train each major muscle group at least twice a week (ACSM 2026).
With equal weekly sets, more sessions barely change growth but help strength.
Full-body A/B gives 2–3 exposures per muscle with 2–3 sessions.
Body-part splits train each muscle only once at this frequency.
Place sessions on non-sport days; keep hard legs away from match eves.

exercises.scenario: You train 3 times a week.

questions.prompt: Which plan gives each muscle 2–3 exposures?
options: Legs three times, upper body never
Chest Monday, back Wednesday, legs Friday
questions.explanation: Every session trains the whole body.

questions.prompt: You miss Wednesday. What's the impact with A/B?
options: Small: nothing goes untrained for a week
You must repeat the whole week
Large: the missed day's muscles go untrained for a whole week
questions.explanation: Each muscle still gets other sessions.

exercises.scenario: With weekly sets equal, one person trains legs once and another twice.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence suggest about muscle growth?
options: The twice-a-week person always grows twice as much muscle
questions.explanation: Volume matters more than how it's split.

options: Once a week is better for strength because of more recovery
Twice a week tends to help

summary.title: A 30-minute session
points: Warm-up 3–5 min, two supersets of compound lifts, accessories, optional finisher.
Warm up specifically: a few dynamic moves, then lighter sets of the first lift.
Main lifts: 3 sets of 8–15 at 1–3 reps in reserve.
About 60–90 s rest after each pair.
Trim accessories first when time is short.

exercises.scenario: You have 22 minutes today instead of 30.

options: The two main supersets, keeping the carries and core work
The warm-up sets of the first lift

questions.prompt: How do you warm up efficiently?
options: Twenty minutes of jogging before every strength session
A few dynamic moves, then lighter sets of the first exercise

exercises.scenario: Your current session is 30 minutes of random exercises.

options: The four-part shape with two compound supersets
Adding a longer cardio warm-up at the start
First, before the main lifts, to warm up the grip

summary.title: Supersets and circuits
points: Supersets alternate two exercises for different muscles; rest after the pair.
They roughly halve time for the same sets (2021 review); better for muscle than max strength.
Circuits: 3+ exercises in a row. EMOM: a set each minute. Density: max good sets in a fixed time.
Pair lower with upper, or push with pull; avoid two grip-heavy moves.

exercises.scenario: You build a superset.

options: One-arm row with farmer's carry, both demanding grip

questions.prompt: You do 5 sets of swings starting each minute. What format is that?
options: A density block with as many sets as possible

exercises.scenario: A friend worries supersets reduce quality.

options: When sets stop being hard or technique slips
Always: supersets never build muscle as well as straight sets
questions.explanation: Time-savers work only if quality holds.

questions.prompt: For which goal are supersets less ideal?
options: Muscle growth, which needs full rest between all sets
questions.explanation: The review favoured them for hypertrophy.

summary.title: Order and rest
points: Strength improved most on the exercise done first; growth didn't depend on order.
Put your priority lift first.
Rest > 60 s may help growth slightly; little extra beyond ~90 s.
1–2 min before repeating a big lift; 60–90 s after a superset pair.
In supersets, the other exercise is part of the rest.

exercises.scenario: This block you most want a stronger split squat.

options: Last, after the carries, so you're warm
Anywhere; order never matters for anything
questions.explanation: Strength improved most on the first exercise.

questions.prompt: How long do you rest before the next split-squat set, with no superset?
options: About 10 seconds to keep the heart rate up
questions.explanation: Big lifts need enough rest to stay hard.

exercises.scenario: A friend rests 30 seconds between all sets to 'burn more fat'.

options: Rest length has no possible effect on anything
Shorter rest always builds more muscle
Resting over 60 s may help growth slightly

questions.prompt: Did exercise order affect muscle growth?
options: Yes, a lot: the first exercise always grows the most
questions.explanation: Order mattered for strength, not growth.

summary.title: Build your week
points: 2–3 full-body A/B sessions on non-sport days.
About 6–10 hard sets per big muscle group a week.
1–3 reps in reserve; supersets; priority lift first; 60–90 s after pairs.
Use the programme builder; run the plan 4–6 weeks while logging.

exercises.scenario: You use the programme builder with no bands or bar.

questions.prompt: What does it do about pulling?
options: Doubles up on rows and suggests bands
Adds pull-ups anyway, since every programme needs them
questions.explanation: Vertical pulling needs a band or bar.

questions.prompt: How long do you run the plan before judging it?
options: One week, then switch if it feels hard
Six months without looking at the log

exercises.scenario: Two weeks in, the plan feels hard and results aren't visible yet.

options: Switch to a new programme you saw online
Full-body A/B 3×/week, 8–10 hard sets per big muscle, 1–3 RIR
Body-part split, 20 sets each to failure, once a week
questions.explanation: All the dials as set in this module.

summary.title: Dials, effort, volume, frequency
points: Seven dials; hard sets per muscle per week is the key number.
Hard sets: 1–3 reps in reserve; failure isn't needed.
Volume: start 6–10 per big muscle a week; more helps with diminishing returns.
Each muscle at least twice a week: full-body A/B.
Change one dial at a time.

exercises.scenario: You plan 3 full-body sessions with 3 squat sets each.

questions.prompt: Weekly hard sets for the legs?
options: 3, since only one session per week counts for each muscle
No, it's far too much for anyone starting out

questions.prompt: Explain why full-body A/B suits 2–3 sessions a week.
questions.modelAnswer: Each session trains every pattern or nearly so, so each big muscle group gets two or three exposures a week, as recommended. A body-part split would train each muscle only once at this frequency, and a missed session would leave a muscle untrained for a week.

exercises.scenario: A friend trains each muscle once a week, every set to failure.

questions.prompt: What two changes does Module 5 suggest?
options: Train each muscle at least twice a week; stop 1–3 reps short
Train each muscle once a month; go past failure with drop sets

questions.prompt: Which is likely to improve more with more frequency at equal volume?
options: Muscle size, which depends mainly on how often you train

summary.title: Building the session and the week
points: 30-minute shape: warm-up, two compound supersets, accessories, finisher.
Supersets halve time for the same sets; pair non-competing muscles.
Priority lift first; 60–90 s after pairs; 1–2 min for big lifts.
Run a plan 4–6 weeks while logging.
The programme builder applies these rules to your kit.

exercises.scenario: You write session B: Bulgarian split squat, floor press, swing, band pulldown, side plank.

options: Split squat + floor press; swing + pulldown; then side plank
All five in a row with no rest
Each exercise alone with 5 minutes rest
Split squat + swing; floor press + pulldown; side plank first
The swing, to raise heart rate
The priority lift, here the split squat
The side plank, to warm up the core
questions.explanation: Strength improves most on what's first.

questions.prompt: Describe your 30-minute session shape with times.
questions.modelAnswer: Warm-up 0–5 min (dynamic moves and ramp-up sets), superset 1 5–14 min (squat + push), superset 2 14–23 min (hinge + pull), accessories 23–28 min (carry or core), optional finisher to 30 min.

exercises.scenario: You're short on time three weeks in a row.

options: Keep accessories and drop the supersets, since they're shorter
Keep the two supersets, drop accessories
questions.explanation: Compound lifts carry most of the training.

questions.prompt: Which format fits a 10-minute emergency session?
options: One superset or an EMOM of swings and push-ups
A full A session done twice as fast with no rest

summary.title: Programme design: the whole picture
points: Seven dials; volume is hard sets per muscle per week.
Effort 1–3 reps in reserve; failure isn't needed.
Start 6–10 sets per big muscle a week; more with diminishing returns.
Each muscle at least twice a week: full-body A/B on non-sport days.
30-minute sessions: two compound supersets, priority lift first, 60–90 s rest.
Run a plan 4–6 weeks, changing one dial at a time.

exercises.scenario: You design your own programme for the next 6 weeks.

options: A five-day body-part split of 30 minutes each, one muscle per day
6–8 reps in reserve to stay fresh
Every set to total failure, with forced extra reps

questions.prompt: How many weekly sets for the legs to start?
options: About 30, to make the most of every week

exercises.scenario: Your old routine: the same 30-minute circuit, no log, mostly cardio.

options: More cardio intervals at the end of each circuit
Planned full-body A/B with counted hard sets
Skipping the main lifts and doing only accessories
questions.explanation: About half the time for the same sets.

questions.prompt: Summarise your programme in one line of dials.
questions.modelAnswer: Full-body A/B, 3 × 30 min a week on non-sport days; per session two supersets of compound lifts, 3 sets of 8–15 at 1–3 reps in reserve, 60–90 s rest after each pair, priority lift first; about 8–10 hard sets per big muscle a week.
